usage: Sits directly before the verb; the default way to mark a large amount
Handy when ordering food or asking a server for more
Before an adjective 많이 shifts from 'a lot' to a degree word, 'very'
너무 많이 마셨어요 = I drank too much; 너무 adds the 'over the line' feeling
examples: 비가 오다 is the set verb for 'it rains'; 많이 measures the quantity
With 좋아하다, 많이 means the feeling is strong, like 'a lot'
Please help yourself / enjoy your meal.
드세요 is the honorific of 먹다; this is what a host warmly says at the table
nuance: 많이 is the adverb form of the adjective 많다 ('to be many/much') and is the everyday word for 'a lot/much', sitting right in front of the verb it modifies (많이 먹어요, 많이 자요). Its near-synonym is 너무: 많이 just states a large amount neutrally, while 너무 carries an 'excessive, over the line' feeling, so 많이 매워요 is 'quite spicy' but 너무 매워요 is 'too spicy (uncomfortably)'. With feeling-verbs and adjectives 많이 stretches to mean 'very/badly', as in 많이 아파요 ('it hurts a lot'). The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the adjective 많다 directly before a verb — you must use the adverb 많이 (많이 먹어요, never 많다 먹어요) — and remembering that, like all Korean adverbs, it comes before the verb, not after it.

mistakes: Using the adjective 많다 where the verb needs the adverb: before a verb it is 많이 먹어요, not 많다 먹어요. 많다 can only sit at the end as a predicate (책이 많아요).
Putting 많이 after the verb on the English word order: 먹어요 많이 sounds broken; Korean adverbs go before the verb (많이 먹어요).
Treating 많이 and 너무 as interchangeable: 너무 implies 'too much/excessive', so 너무 좋아요 ('I like it so much') and 많이 좋아요 carry slightly different feelings.

english: a little, a bit, a few
usage: The exact opposite of 많이; requests a small amount
Before an adjective it softens the degree to 'a bit'
조금만 기다려 주세요 = please wait just a moment; 만 ('only') caps it small
A fixed time phrase meaning 'a moment ago'
examples: The perfect modest answer for a beginner; 조금 lowers the claim
조금 before the verb marks a small quantity of the object
조금 softens 피곤하다 so you don't overstate it
nuance: 조금 means 'a little / a bit / a few' and is the natural counterweight to 많이 for small amounts or mild degrees. Its closest relative is its own contracted form 좀: 조금 is the full, slightly more careful version you can write and say, while 좀 is the quick spoken reduction (조금만요 ↔ 좀만요 are the same idea). Compared with the noun-ish 약간 ('slightly', a touch more formal/written), 조금 is the warm conversational choice. It naturally collocates with quantities and gentle states — 조금 더 ('a little more'), 조금 있다가 ('in a little while') — and its softness makes it ideal for modest answers and polite requests. The English-speaker pitfall is hearing 좀 in speech and not realizing it is just 조금 reduced, and over-stacking it with big-amount words: 조금 많이 is self-contradictory because 조금 only ever points to a small degree.

usage: The short, spoken reduction of 조금
Here 좀 is a softener, not really an amount, like a gentle 'please'
Extremely common when ordering or asking for things at a shop
잠깐만요 buys a moment of time; pairs naturally with 좀 in requests
examples: It's a bit cold in here.
좀 makes the comment sound soft and offhand rather than a complaint
Slipping in 좀 makes the request friendlier and more natural than 물 주세요
좀 cushions a refusal so it lands gently
nuance: 좀 is the contracted, spoken form of 조금 and is everywhere in daily conversation. Its key second life — the part that trips up English speakers — is as a request softener: in 물 좀 주세요 or 좀 도와주세요, 좀 is not measuring a 'little' amount at all but functioning like 'please/if you would', taking the bluntness off a command. So 물 주세요 is grammatically fine but can feel abrupt, whereas 물 좀 주세요 sounds warm and natural. Compared with the full 조금, 좀 is purely conversational and a touch more casual; in formal writing or stiff announcements you revert to 조금 or a fuller polite request form. Collocates constantly with request verbs (좀 주세요, 좀 해 주세요, 좀 보여 주세요) and with mild complaints (좀 춥다, 좀 그렇다). The pitfall is over-literal reading: don't try to translate the 'softener' 좀 as 'a little', and don't drop it from requests — Koreans add it precisely to sound polite.

usage: Right before the verb; signals the action is complete or the whole thing covered
Everything is fine / I'm good with all of it
I did it all / I'm done
The natural way to report finishing a task
거의 다 왔어요 = we're almost there; 거의 ('nearly') tempers 다
examples: 다 + 했어요 says the whole thing is complete
What you say when your plate is empty
Here 다 covers 'all of them', the people, not completion
nuance: 다 is a small but powerful native word meaning 'all / everything / completely', placed directly before the verb. It carries two senses that context separates: completion of an action (다 했어요 = 'all done', the task is finished) and total coverage of a group (다 왔어요 = 'everyone came'). Its near-synonym is the fuller 모두; 다 is the short, ultra-frequent spoken default, while 모두 is a touch more deliberate and can also stand alone as a noun ('everyone'). A subtle bonus sense is 'about to be used up/finished' — 시간 다 됐어요 ('time's up'). The classic English-speaker pitfalls are mixing the look-alike one-syllable adverbs (다 'all' vs 또 'again' vs 더 'more'), and English word order: 다 must precede the verb (다 먹었어요), never follow it.

Reading every 다 as 'completely' when it often means 'all of them (people/things)': 친구들이 다 왔어요 is about everyone, not about thoroughness.

usage: A clearer, fuller 'all/everyone' than the terse 다
모두 합쳐서 얼마예요? = how much for everything together?
여러분 모두 환영해요 = welcome, everyone; 모두 trails the noun as 'all'
Stacking 모두 + 다 adds emphasis: 'all of it, the whole lot'
examples: There are four of us in my family.
모두 sums up a total head count, 'in all'
모두 as a noun addressing the whole group
모두 here covers 'all of them' as an adverb
nuance: 모두 means 'all / everyone / in total' and feels a notch fuller, clearer, and slightly more formal than the very short native 다. Its distinctive trait — and the reason to learn it alongside 다 — is its flexibility of part of speech: it can be a noun ('everyone': 모두 환영해요, 모두의 꿈 'everyone's dream') or an adverb ('all': 모두 모였어요), whereas 다 leans adverbial. Near-synonyms split by feel: 다 is the quick everyday choice, 모두 is the cleaner one for counting or addressing a whole group, and 전부 ('the entirety/the whole') stresses 'every last bit' and pairs well with things and totals. It collocates with gatherings, totals, and greetings (모두 모이다, 모두 합쳐서, 여러분 모두). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 모두 is only an adverb and only for people; it also stands as a noun and freely covers things and sums (모두 합쳐서).

mistakes: Assuming 모두 is only an adverb: it can stand as a noun meaning 'everyone' (모두 안녕하세요, 모두의 의견 'everyone's opinion').
Restricting 모두 to people: it equally covers things and totals, as in 모두 합쳐서 ('all together in total') or 짐을 모두 챙겼어요 ('I packed all the bags').
Treating 모두 and 다 as identical in register: 다 is the casual spoken default, while 모두 sounds a touch fuller and fits writing or addressing a crowd.

usage: A clear, slightly polished way to say 'together'
A common, warm invitation to share a meal
친구와 함께 = together with a friend; needs the 와/과 particle
다 함께 노래해요 = let's all sing together; 다 + 함께 = everyone, together
examples: Let's watch a movie together this weekend.
함께 before the verb means 'do it together'
I had dinner with my family.
The pattern is N과 함께 = 'together with N'
A friendly suggestion to a classmate; 함께 sounds inclusive and warm
nuance: 함께 means 'together / along with' and is the slightly warmer, more polished sibling of the everyday 같이. The two overlap almost completely in meaning, but they differ in feel and grammar habits: 같이 is the casual spoken default and also doubles as 'like/as' with 처럼-style nouns (눈같이 'like snow'), whereas 함께 is purely 'together', sounds a touch softer and more heartfelt, and shows up in invitations, slogans, and announcements (함께 가요, 함께 만들어요 'let's build it together'). Both commonly take the particle 와/과 (or casual 하고/랑) to name the companion: 친구와 함께, 가족과 함께. The English-speaker pitfall is dropping that particle — 'with my friend' must be 친구와 함께, not 친구 함께 — and assuming 함께 and 같이 are sharply different when they are really register twins, with 함께 just sounding a shade more polished.

mistakes: Treating 함께 and 같이 as sharply different words: they overlap closely; 함께 just sounds a bit softer and more polished, 같이 a bit more casual.
Omitting the particle 와/과 before 함께 when naming the companion: it is 친구와 함께, not 친구 함께.
Forgetting 같이 has an extra 'like/as' meaning that 함께 lacks: 별같이 빛나다 ('shine like a star') cannot use 함께.

english: just, simply, for no special reason
usage: Means 'simply' doing something, nothing special going on
I just feel kind of off
A vague, soft way to avoid a full explanation
Here it means 'plain / without changes / as-is'
examples: I just want to rest today.
그냥 softens it to 'simply rest, nothing planned'
I just asked, no special reason.
A very common casual cushion for a question
For coffee, just a plain americano, please.
nuance: 그냥 means 'just / simply / for no particular reason' and is one of the most useful filler-style words in casual Korean, prized because it lets you decline to over-explain. Its sense flexes with context: 'simply, with no agenda' (그냥 집에 있어요), 'plain / as it is, unchanged' (그냥 주세요, 그냥 아메리카노), and the stand-alone 'no reason' reply (왜? 그냥). Its near-neighbor 그저 ('merely, simply') is more literary and emphatic, while 막 ('just, randomly/recklessly') is rougher and busier — so 그냥 is the gentle, neutral middle. It collocates with low-key states and soft hedges (그냥 좀 그래요, 그냥 그래요 'it's so-so', 그냥 한번 'just once for the heck of it'). The English-speaker pitfall is hunting for one fixed translation — 'just' won't always fit — and over-using it in formal or business contexts, where its vagueness can read as evasive or unpolished.

Over-using 그냥 in formal or business settings: it is casual and its vagueness can sound evasive; a fuller explanation fits there.
Confusing 그냥 with 그래서 ('so/therefore') because both start with 그: they are unrelated — 그냥 means 'just', 그래서 links cause and result.

usage: Adds a firm, sincere promise to the verb
Stresses that something is genuinely essential
examples: I'll be sure to call tomorrow.
꼭 makes the promise sound committed, not casual
Make sure to take your medicine.
A caring reminder; 꼭 = without fail
Let's definitely go together next time.
nuance: 꼭 means 'definitely / for sure / without fail' and injects strong intention or a firm request into a sentence: with promises it sounds sincere and committed (꼭 갈게요), and with requests it makes them warm but insistent (꼭 오세요). Its near-synonym 반드시 carries the same 'without fail' core but is more formal, rule-like, and written (regulations and warnings favor 반드시 …해야 한다), whereas 꼭 is the warmer, more personal everyday choice; 절대 is its negative-side cousin ('absolutely not', 절대 안 돼요). 꼭 also has a secondary 'exactly/just like' sense (꼭 엄마 같아요 'just like Mom'), though learners use the 'for sure' meaning most. The English-speaker pitfall is the look-alike/sound-alike 곧 ('soon'): 꼭 갈게요 ('I'll definitely go') is a promise of certainty, while 곧 갈게요 ('I'll go soon') is about timing — keep the tense 꼭 distinct from the timing 곧.

usage: The time sense: immediately, with no delay
The location sense: points to an exact spot
바로 앞에 있어요 = it's right in front; 바로 pins the position
examples: 지금 바로 = right this very moment, no waiting
The school is right next to my house.
바로 before the verb signals immediacy
nuance: 바로 carries two everyday senses split by context: 'right away / immediately' with actions (바로 가요, 바로 출발해요) and 'exactly / right (there)' with places and identifications (바로 여기, 바로 앞, 바로 그거예요). For the time sense, its near-synonym 곧 means 'soon / shortly' — a small gap remains — while 바로 means truly 'this instant, with zero delay', so 바로 가요 is more immediate than 곧 가요. For the location/identification sense, 바로 tightens 'next to/in front of' into 'directly, precisely' and has no single English twin; it behaves like 'right' in 'right next to'. It collocates tightly with position words (바로 옆/앞/뒤/위) and with emphatic confirmations (바로 그거, 바로 너 'you, exactly'). The English-speaker pitfall is assuming 바로 only means 'immediately' and missing its 'exactly/right-there' use, plus stranding it from the word it marks — keep 바로 hugging the verb or noun (바로 앞, not 앞 바로).

usage: The default word for doing an action fast
Doubled for emphasis; a famous shorthand for the Korean pace of life
더 빨리 해 주세요 = please do it faster; 더 ('more') raises the speed
examples: Hurry up, the bus is coming!
Everyday urging when you're in a rush
빨리 before the verb describes the speed of the action
A caring set phrase to someone who is sick; 낫다 ('heal') is ㅅ-irregular
nuance: 빨리 means 'quickly / fast', the adverb derived from the adjective 빠르다 ('to be fast'), and is among the first action adverbs a beginner needs. Doubled as 빨리빨리, it famously captures the Korean 'hurry, hurry' tempo and adds real urgency. Watch the synonym line with 일찍: 빨리 is about speed ('do it fast'), while 일찍 is about an early point in time ('early'), so 빨리 일어났어요 means 'I got up fast' but 일찍 일어났어요 means 'I got up early' — English 'quick/early' blurs this. The deeper pitfall is the adverb-vs-adjective split: from the stem 빠르- you use the adverb 빨리 before a verb (빨리 먹어요), but to describe a noun you must switch to the adjective form 빠른 (빠른 차 'a fast car') — never 빨리 차. 빠르다 is a 르-irregular, so its polite form is 빨라요. It collocates with motion and effort verbs (빨리 가다/오다/하다) and warm wishes (빨리 나으세요).

usage: Fuller and warmer than the plain 더
Doubling to 더욱더 pushes the increase strongly
A kind, slightly formal good wish
examples: I'll work even harder from now on.
날씨가 더우니까 물을 더욱 많이 마셔요.
Since it's hot, drink even more water.
After practicing, it got even better.
더욱 marks a further step up from before
nuance: 더욱 means 'even more / all the more' and is the fuller, warmer, slightly more formal cousin of the basic comparative adverb 더 ('more'). The two share a core, but they split by register and rhythm: 더 is the plain everyday workhorse (더 주세요 'give me more'), while 더욱 adds a literary, heartfelt lift and shows up in earnest statements, speeches, and good wishes (더욱 노력할게요, 더욱 건강하세요), with the reduplicated 더욱더 cranking the emphasis higher still. A neighboring word, 한층 ('a notch more'), is similarly elevated and written. 더욱 collocates with effort, improvement, and wishes (더욱 열심히, 더욱 좋아지다, 더욱 발전하다). The English-speaker pitfall is over-using 더욱 in casual chat or texting, where it sounds stiff — there you just say 더 — and assuming it is a wholly separate word from 더 rather than its more polished register-partner.

usage: A warm, gentle 'really', softer than 너무
A sincere compliment with a kind tone
참 standing alone flags a sudden 'oh, that reminds me'
examples: The weather is really lovely today.
참 lends a soft, sincere, almost admiring feeling
Your Korean pronunciation is really good.
A warm, genuine compliment; pairs well with 네요
Oh, by the way, are you free tomorrow?
참 as a 'that just reminded me' opener
nuance: 참 means 'really / truly / quite' but with a gentle, sincere, faintly admiring warmth that makes it lovely for heartfelt compliments (참 좋아요, 참 예뻐요, 참 착하다 'so kind'). Its register is the dividing line against its near-synonyms: 너무 is strong and can tip into 'too much', 정말/진짜 are emphatic 'really!', while 참 is the soft, warm, slightly old-fashioned 'really' that sounds caring rather than intense — elders use it often. A completely separate, very common use is the stand-alone interjection 참! meaning 'oh, that reminds me!' when something pops into your head mid-conversation. It collocates with gentle praise and pleasant states (참 좋다, 참 예쁘다, 참 잘했어요 'well done'). The English-speaker pitfall is expecting 참 to hit hard like 너무 and being puzzled by its softness, and reading the interjection 참! as an intensifier when it actually signals a sudden memory.

usage: Describes filling a container right to the top
방이 사람으로 가득 찼어요 = the room is packed with people
가득 담아 주세요 = please fill it right up
Standard at a gas station: 가득이요 = full tank
examples: I poured the cup full of water.
가득 = right up to the brim
The mart is packed with people.
가득하다 = to be full/packed; 가득 + 하다
Please fill it all the way.
Useful at a gas station or when asking for a full serving
nuance: 가득 means 'fully / full to the brim' and specifically describes a container, space, or even a feeling being filled completely — its meaning is about capacity reached, not just quantity. This is the key line against its near-synonym 많이: 많이 marks 'a large amount' in general (많이 먹어요 'eat a lot'), while 가득 says 'filled to the limit', so 컵에 물이 가득 means the cup is brimming, not merely that there is much water around. It pairs habitually with filling verbs — 채우다 ('fill'), 차다 ('become full'), 담다 ('put in'), 넣다 ('insert') — and the bound form 가득하다 means 'to be full/packed' (사람으로 가득하다). It also extends to emotion (행복이 가득하다 'full of happiness'). A handy real-life anchor is the gas station, where 가득이요 means 'fill the tank'. The English-speaker pitfall is using 가득 as a general 'a lot' with any verb; it only fits filling/packing situations, so 가득 먹어요 sounds odd where you want 많이 먹어요.

usage: 푹 쉬세요 = rest up well, a caring set phrase
푹 잤어요 = I slept deeply and well
In cooking: boil slowly until soft and rich
드라마에 푹 빠졌어요 = I'm totally hooked on the drama
examples: Please rest up well at home today.
A warm thing to say to someone who's tired or unwell
I slept soundly yesterday, so I feel refreshed.
푹 자다 = sleep deeply; pairs with feeling 개운하다
For a cold, resting well is best.
nuance: 푹 is a vivid native mimetic adverb (의태어) meaning doing something deeply, soundly, and thoroughly, and it lives most in the caring collocations 푹 쉬다 ('rest well') and 푹 자다 ('sleep soundly'), which beginners hear constantly as warm wishes. Unlike a general intensifier such as 많이 ('a lot') or 잘 ('well'), 푹 adds a specific texture of 'completely, comfortably, all the way down' — 푹 자다 isn't just sleeping much, it's sleeping deep and restoring. It splits into a few homes: rest/sleep (푹 쉬다/자다), slow cooking ('simmer until tender', 푹 끓이다/삶다), and the figurative 푹 빠지다 ('be totally absorbed/hooked'). It also describes sinking softly into something (소파에 푹 파묻히다). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 푹 as an all-purpose 'very'; it is not — it specifically means 'deeply/soundly/thoroughly' and only suits resting, sleeping, simmering, and being absorbed. Above all, memorize the everyday set phrase 푹 쉬세요, the natural way to tell someone to rest up.
